brief.headline: Offer to pay them in 15 days instead of 30 — their cash is stuck for 101 days (vs 64 peers) and they borrow at 12.16%, so win a 6% price cut in return.

priceAsk.summary: Ask for a 6% price cut in exchange for paying in 15 days instead of 30
priceAsk.target: A discount roughly matching their borrowing cost of 12.16% (half that for 15-day acceleration = ~6%)
priceAsk.basis: Their cash is stuck for 101 days vs 64 for similar firms, and they borrow money at 12.16%. Paying them 15 days earlier frees up their cash and saves them interest — that's worth about 6% to them. Our current price sits at the top of the fair market band (₹205–305/kg, typical ₹250/kg), so there's room to move down while staying market-fair.

paymentTermAsk.summary: Offer to pay in 15 days (15 days faster than today's 30) in exchange for the price cut
paymentTermAsk.cashImpact: This costs us ₹26.60 L in cash we'll pay sooner, but we win it back many times over through the 6% saving on ₹6.47 Cr annual spend (roughly ₹39 L/year).

brief.financialLeverage: Shrinath is a ₹1064.86 Cr company, so our ₹6.47 Cr (0.61% of their revenue) is small to them — we have limited volume leverage. But their finances are tight: they keep only 2.3% profit (vs 2.5% peers), owe 1.25× their own cash, and their cash is stuck for 101 days (vs 64 peers) — much longer than similar firms. They borrow at 12.16%, so cash is expensive for them. They also take 51 days to pay their own suppliers (vs 40 peers), showing they're already stretching payment. All this means they will value faster payment highly — use that to win the price cut, but don't push so hard on price alone that you squeeze their thin 2.3% margin and risk supply (their credit rating is middling CARE BBB+ / Stable, and they sit in the grey zone on distress risk with an Altman Z of 2.36).

evidence.point: Their cash is stuck much longer than peers
They borrow money at a high rate, so early payment is valuable to them
They already pay their own suppliers slower than peers
They keep very little profit, so a big price squeeze could hurt supply
We are a small customer to them

alternates.name: Huhtamaki India Ltd
alternates.why: Listed flexible-packaging converter already supplying FDC in small volumes — a proven, scalable second source for laminate sachets that can take more volume if Shrinath stumbles.

alternates.name: UFLEX Ltd
alternates.why: Listed flexibles giant that makes both film substrate and converts it into laminates — can second-source at scale and gives us leverage on both material and conversion price.

alternates.name: Constantia Parikh Packaging Pvt Ltd
alternates.why: Part of the global Constantia group, converts pharma blister and sachet laminates — strong second-source capability, though their own health score is weaker (D, 31/100) so qualify carefully before moving volume.

risks: Their credit rating is middling (CARE BBB+ / Stable) and they sit in the grey zone on distress risk (Altman Z 2.36) — don't squeeze so hard that you tip a fragile supplier over; keep the tone collaborative and frame the faster payment as help.
They have EPF payment delays on record — a compliance red flag that could signal cash strain or management distraction; monitor closely and keep the second source warm.
Their profit margin is only 2.3% — pushing price too hard without giving them the payment-speed benefit could eat into that thin cushion and risk supply stability.
We're only 0.61% of their revenue, so we have little volume leverage — lead with the win-win (faster payment) rather than trying to strong-arm them on price alone.
brief.suggestedOpeningLine: We'd like to help free up your cash by paying you in 15 days instead of 30 — and in return, we're looking for a price adjustment that reflects the interest saving that gives you.
